explain.say: The end of each bone is capped with cartilage, a smooth, rubbery tissue. It is slipperier than ice on ice and acts as a cushion when you land on your feet.

explain.say: Between the caps is a thin film of synovial fluid, a slippery liquid like egg white. It oils the surfaces and feeds the cartilage, which has no blood vessels of its own.

explain.say: A tough bag called the joint capsule wraps the whole joint and holds the fluid in. Its inner lining makes the synovial fluid, and ligaments outside hold the bones in line.

faq.a: Synovial fluid is a thick, slippery liquid inside moving joints. It lubricates the cartilage so the bones glide, and it carries nutrients to the cartilage.
asks: Tell me about the synovial fluid

faq.q: What does cartilage do in a joint?
faq.a: Cartilage covers the ends of bones in a joint. It is smooth and slippery, so bones glide easily, and slightly squashy, so it absorbs shocks.
asks: Tell me about the cartilage cap

faq.a: Because their ends are coated with smooth cartilage and oiled by synovial fluid. Together they make friction in a healthy joint lower than ice sliding on ice.
It is a tough, sleeve-like bag around a moving joint. It holds the joint together and its lining, the synovial membrane, makes the synovial fluid.
asks: What holds the fluid in a joint?

faq.a: When a joint is stretched, the pressure in the synovial fluid drops and a gas bubble forms quickly, which makes the pop. It takes a while before the joint can crack again.
asks: What is the cracking sound in joints?

facts: Joint cartilage has no blood vessels; it gets nutrients from the synovial fluid.
The friction between cartilage surfaces in a healthy joint is lower than that of ice sliding on ice.

quiz.why: The synovial membrane lining the joint capsule produces the fluid.

wrong.1: Bone marrow makes blood cells, not joint fluid.
wrong.2: The stomach makes digestive juice, not joint fluid.
